description: Team with creative and strong technical skills.
summary:
OutpostOS is a browser-based, team-based game that lets students aged 10-16 run a lunar or Martian outpost. Players balance five linked systems: power, life support, radiation shielding, food production and thermal control. Each “sol” (Martian day), they plan their resources, face a random event such as a solar flare or dust storm, and watch the results live.

The game addresses the challenge through its Cascade Engine, where every decision affects the other systems. More shielding costs power, which means fewer grow lights and less food. Students feel real engineering trade-offs without needing advanced knowledge. When a mission fails, a Failure Replay rewinds the game and highlights the exact chain of decisions behind the failure, like a real post-mortem. Crew roles let each student manage one console, so teams must negotiate shared limits.

This matters because real missions fail through chains of linked decisions, not single mistakes. OutpostOS makes that idea tangible and fun, building systems thinking, budgeting and data-based decision-making. It runs offline on ordinary school laptops and fits in a 20-minute class session.
details:
Live project: https://outpostos-bzctr8ty.manus.game

What it does and how it works
OutpostOS is a browser-based game in which students aged 10-16 run a 4-person Moon base for 30 sols (Martian days). Each sol, the player shares limited power between four systems: Life Support, Radiation Shield, Food Farm and Thermal Control. Solar power is available by day and absent at night, and the battery stores spare energy. A seeded random generator adds events such as solar flares, dust storms, oxygen leaks and crop blight, with a forecast of tomorrow’s event so students can plan ahead. The systems are linked (the Cascade Engine): a power shortfall weakens every system, and a cold base halves crop growth. If the crew fails, the Failure Replay shows the root cause and the last 6 sols in a table, with the row where the chain began highlighted. Students can replay the same mission and fix that decision. An Engineer Notebook logs every sol automatically.

Benefits and intended impact
Students learn systems thinking, resource budgeting and evidence-based decision-making by experiencing real trade-offs, not reading about them. The game fits a 20-minute class period and runs in any browser on school laptops and phones. Our aim is to make students ask “why did it fail?” and then fix it, which is how real engineers work.

Tools and technology
HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with a deterministic simulation so any mission can be replayed exactly. The project is hosted online at the link above. Code and text were drafted with AI tools (Claude by Anthropic), then reviewed, tested and edited by our team.

Creativity
Most space games reward a high score. OutpostOS rewards understanding: the failure analysis is the main learning moment, and the game makes the chain of cause and effect visible. Two levels (Cadet with hints, Pilot without) suit different ages.

Factors we considered

  • Age-appropriate difficulty and a short session length
  • Scientific realism versus simplicity (values are simplified, and we label them as such)
  • Accessibility on low-spec devices and mobile screens
  • Fairness and replayability through seeded events
  • Planned next steps: crew-role co-op mode, a teacher dashboard, a Mars scenario, and Tamil and Hindi support
